title: Tame Startup Apps
overview: Most slow boots are just too many programs launching at login. Disabling startup entries you do not need is the fastest, safest speedup in Windows — and it is fully reversible.

demo.code:
# Audit startup impact (PowerShell)
Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Select Name, Command, Location | Format-Table -AutoSize
# High-impact auto-starts via registry Run keys:
Get-ItemProperty "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell — review the list, then disable in Task Manager

steps: Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) > Startup apps tab
Sort by Startup impact; disable everything marked High that you do not need at boot (updaters, chat apps, game launchers)
Settings > Apps > Startup: same list, friendlier switches
Keep enabled: antivirus, audio, hardware utilities. Disable: anything you can launch manually
Reboot and time the difference

commands.taskmgr_startup: Task Manager > Startup apps > right-click > Disable
commands.measure: Measure boot: Task Manager > Startup apps shows "Last BIOS time"

expected_gain: Boot time often cut 30-60%; less RAM used at idle
risk: Low — disabling startup never uninstalls anything; re-enable any time
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Remove Bloatware and Preinstalled Apps
overview: New PCs ship with trials, vendor utilities, and apps you will never open — all consuming disk, RAM, and startup time. Removing them is safe if you stick to obvious non-system apps.

demo.code:
# List installed apps by size, spot the bloat (PowerShell)
Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*" |
  Where-Object { $_.DisplayName } |
  Select DisplayName, @{n="SizeMB";e={[math]::Round($_.EstimatedSize/1024,1)}} |
  Sort-Object SizeMB -Descending | Select -First 20 | Format-Table -AutoSize
# remove a Store app (example):
# Get-AppxPackage *CandyCrush* | Remove-AppxPackage
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell; uninstall from Settings or with winget

steps: Settings > Apps > Installed apps: sort by size; uninstall obvious bloat (trials, vendor games, duplicate utilities)
For stubborn preinstalled Store apps, use winget: winget list, then winget uninstall <name>
Do NOT remove: drivers, chipset software, .NET/VC++ runtimes, or anything with Microsoft/Intel/AMD/NVIDIA in the name unless you know why
Reboot after a batch
expected_gain: Freed disk space; fewer background processes; cleaner Start menu
risk: Low if you avoid drivers and system components
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Disk Cleanup and Storage Sense
overview: Windows accumulates gigabytes of temp files, update leftovers, and caches. Disk Cleanup plus Storage Sense automates the purge safely — never "cleaner" apps of dubious origin.

demo.code:
REM Safe disk cleanup (elevated)
cleanmgr /sageset:1
REM tick the boxes once, then run silently on schedule:
REM cleanmgr /sagerun:1
REM component store cleanup:
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup
REM show largest folders on C: (PowerShell):
REM Get-ChildItem C:\ -Directory ^| ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{Dir=$_.Name; GB=[math]::Round((Get-ChildItem $_.FullName -Recurse -File -EA SilentlyContinue ^| Measure-Object Length -Sum).Sum/1GB,2)} } ^| Sort GB -Desc ^| Select -First 10
demo.how_to_run: Run in an elevated Command Prompt

steps: Run Disk Cleanup: cleanmgr.exe — check Temporary files, Recycle Bin, Thumbnails
Click "Clean up system files" and add Windows Update Cleanup, Previous Windows installations
Enable Storage Sense: Settings > System > Storage > on; configure to run weekly and empty Recycle Bin after 30 days
Check the big hitters: Settings > System > Storage shows what uses space
expected_gain: Commonly 5-30 GB recovered; updates install more reliably
risk: Low — only temp/update leftovers are removed
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: High-Performance Power Plan
overview: Windows power plans trade speed for battery/heat. On desktops — and plugged-in laptops doing heavy work — the High performance plan stops the CPU from napping mid-task.

demo.code:
REM Power plan control
powercfg /list
REM activate High performance (use the GUID from /list):
REM powercfg /setactive 8c5e7fda-e8bf-4a96-9a85-a6e23a8c635c
REM add the Ultimate Performance plan:
powercfg -duplicatescheme e9a42b02-d5df-448d-aa00-03f14749eb61
REM battery report (laptops):
powercfg /batteryreport /output "%USERPROFILE%\Desktop\battery-report.html"
demo.how_to_run: Run in Command Prompt (activation needs elevation)

steps: Settings > System > Power & battery > Power mode: Best performance (laptops)
Desktops: Control Panel > Power Options > High performance
Laptops on battery: keep Balanced — High performance drains fast
Advanced: Processor power management > Minimum 5%, Maximum 100%
expected_gain: Snappier heavy workloads; fewer micro-stutters on desktops
risk: Low — more heat/noise and battery drain on laptops
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Update GPU and Chipset Drivers
overview: Fresh GPU drivers bring game performance and fix stutters; chipset drivers fix USB, sleep, and storage weirdness. Get them from the vendor — not random "driver updater" tools.

demo.code:
# Driver versions at a glance (PowerShell)
Get-CimInstance Win32_VideoController | Select Name, DriverVersion
Get-PnpDevice -Class System | Where-Object { $_.FriendlyName -like "*chipset*" -or $_.FriendlyName -like "*SMBus*" } | Select FriendlyName, Status
# NVIDIA quick check:
# nvidia-smi
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell

steps: GPU: NVIDIA GeForce Experience / AMD Adrenalin / Intel Arc — clean-install the latest
Chipset: motherboard vendor support page > chipset driver
Use DDU in Safe Mode only if the GPU driver is corrupt
Reboot after each; verify in Device Manager (no yellow warnings)

commands.ddu: Display Driver Uninstaller in Safe Mode (corrupt installs only)
commands.verify: Device Manager > Display adapters > Properties > Driver version

expected_gain: Game FPS gains on new titles; fewer crashes and stutters
risk: Medium — a bad GPU install can black-screen; keep DDU + known-good driver on USB
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Upgrade to an SSD: The Priority Guide
title: Upgrade to an SSD: The Priority Guide
overview: If your PC still boots Windows from a spinning hard drive, an SSD is the single biggest speedup available — bigger than CPU or RAM upgrades. Clone or clean-install; either way the difference is night and day.

demo.code:
# Confirm drive types + health before buying (elevated)
Get-PhysicalDisk | Select FriendlyName, MediaType, HealthStatus, OperationalStatus, Size
# rough disk speed test (built in):
winsat diskformal
demo.how_to_run: Run in elevated PowerShell

steps: Confirm you have an HDD: Task Manager > Performance > Disk (HDD vs SSD)
Buy a SATA SSD (any PC) or NVMe SSD (if your board has an M.2 slot) — 500 GB minimum for Windows
Clone with the SSD vendor’s free tool (Samsung Magician, Crucial, Macrium) or clean-install Windows
Set the SSD first in BIOS boot order
Keep the HDD as bulk storage

commands.clone: Vendor cloning tool from a USB-boot or second PC

expected_gain: Boot 2-5x faster; apps launch instantly; 100%-disk problems vanish
risk: Medium — back up before cloning; verify the clone boots before wiping the old drive
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Add RAM: How Much Is Enough
title: Add RAM: How Much Is Enough
overview: RAM upgrades help only if you are actually running out. Check first: sustained high memory use with disk thrashing means more RAM helps; otherwise spend the money on an SSD.

demo.code:
# RAM inventory (PowerShell)
Get-CimInstance Win32_PhysicalMemory | Select Manufacturer, Capacity, Speed, SMBIOSMemoryType
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select TotalPhysicalMemory
# memory pressure right now:
Get-Counter "\Memory\Available MBytes"
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell

steps: Task Manager > Performance > Memory: if Committed routinely exceeds physical RAM, you need more
8 GB: minimum for comfortable Windows; 16 GB: the sweet spot; 32 GB: creators/VMs
Match: DDR4 vs DDR5, speed, and ideally identical sticks (check CPU-Z or the manual)
Enable XMP/DOCP in BIOS after installing to get rated speed
Laptops: check if RAM is soldered before buying

commands.check: Task Manager > Performance > Memory (slots used, speed)
commands.xmp: Enable in BIOS > AI Tweaker/OC > XMP/DOCP

expected_gain: Eliminates swapping stutter when RAM was the bottleneck; no gain if it was not
risk: Low — buy the right DDR generation; ground yourself during install
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Defrag HDDs, TRIM SSDs
overview: Spinning disks fragment; SSDs do not need defragging and are harmed by it. Windows handles both automatically — your job is just to verify the schedule is on and not "optimizing" the SSD wrongly.

demo.code:
REM Verify TRIM + scheduled optimization
fsutil behavior query DisableDeleteNotify
REM 0 = TRIM enabled (good). 1 = disabled.
defrag C: /O
REM /O = retrim (safe for SSDs). Never use /D defrag on SSD.
REM open the GUI:
REM dfrgui.exe
demo.how_to_run: Run in an elevated Command Prompt

steps: Search "Defragment": open Optimize Drives
HDD: ensure Scheduled optimization is On (weekly)
SSD: Windows runs TRIM automatically — do NOT defrag it manually
If an SSD shows "Needs optimization", let TRIM run; check again tomorrow

commands.trim_check: fsutil behavior query DisableDeleteNotify (0 = TRIM on)

expected_gain: HDDs regain sequential speed; SSDs stay fast via TRIM
risk: Low — never run classic defrag on an SSD
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Tune Virtual Memory (Pagefile)
overview: The pagefile is Windows’ overflow for RAM. On systems with 16 GB+ RAM and an SSD, the defaults are fine; on tight-RAM HDD systems, a fixed-size pagefile stops fragmentation stutter.

demo.code:
# Current pagefile config (PowerShell)
Get-CimInstance Win32_PageFileSetting | Select Name, InitialSize, MaximumSize
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select AutomaticManagedPagefile
# memory pressure:
Get-Counter "\Paging File(_Total)\% Usage"
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell

steps: System > Advanced system settings > Performance Settings > Advanced > Virtual memory
Uncheck "Automatically manage" only if you know why
Rule of thumb: fixed pagefile of 1x RAM on HDD systems short on RAM; system-managed is fine on 16 GB+ SSD systems
Set on the fastest drive; keep at least 800 MB on C: for crash dumps
expected_gain: Modest — mainly stability on RAM-starved systems
risk: Medium — too-small pagefile causes out-of-memory crashes; when in doubt leave automatic
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Disable Telemetry and Background Apps
overview: Windows runs background tasks — telemetry, suggestions, background Store apps — that cost CPU, RAM, and disk. Trimming the obvious ones is safe; registry hacks from the internet are not.

demo.code:
# Audit background-capable Store apps (PowerShell)
Get-AppxPackage | Select Name, PackageFullName | Sort-Object Name | Format-Table -AutoSize
# check the telemetry service state:
Get-Service DiagTrack | Select Name, Status, StartType
# set to Manual (safer than Disabled):
# Set-Service DiagTrack -StartupType Manual
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell; change startup types cautiously

steps: Settings > Privacy & security > Background apps: turn off apps you never use
Settings > Privacy: disable advertising ID, tailored experiences, suggested content
Task Scheduler: disable Customer Experience Improvement Program tasks (careful, one by one)
Avoid random "debloat scripts" — they break updates and are hard to undo

commands.background: Settings > Apps > Installed apps > ... > Advanced options > Background apps permissions
commands.services: services.msc — set "Connected User Experiences and Telemetry" to Manual (not Disabled)

expected_gain: Less idle CPU/disk; slightly longer battery life
risk: Medium — aggressive scripts break Windows Update; stick to Settings toggles
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Browser Cleanup: Extensions and Cache
overview: A browser with 30 extensions and gigabytes of cache feels slow because it is slow. Extension audit + cache clear restores speed without losing anything important.

demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell — big numbers mean heavy caches

steps: Open extensions page (chrome://extensions, edge://extensions, about:addons): remove anything you do not recognize or no longer use
Clear cached images/files (keep passwords/history): Settings > Privacy > Clear browsing data
Disable "continue running background apps" if you close the browser fully
Compare: test the same site in a fresh profile to prove extensions were the drag
expected_gain: Faster page loads; less RAM per tab
risk: Low
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Game Mode and Hardware-Accelerated GPU Scheduling
title: Game Mode and Hardware-Accelerated GPU Scheduling
overview: Two Windows toggles that help gaming: Game Mode (deprioritizes background work) and Hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling (cuts latency). Both are safe one-click changes.

demo.code:
# Verify the toggles (PowerShell)
Get-ItemProperty "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\GameBar" -Name AllowAutoGameMode -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\GraphicsDrivers" -Name HwSchMode -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
# HwSchMode 2 = HAGS on (needs reboot after change)
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell

steps: Settings > Gaming > Game Mode: On
Settings > System > Display > Graphics > Change default graphics settings: Hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling On (reboot)
In the same page: add your game, set to High performance
Keep GPU drivers current — these features depend on them

commands.hags: Settings > System > Display > Graphics > Default graphics settings

expected_gain: 1-5% FPS and smoother frametimes on supported hardware
risk: Low
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Disable Search Indexing on SSDs
overview: Windows Search indexing hammers disks building its index. On SSDs, searches are already fast — disabling the indexer saves writes and background CPU with little downside.

demo.code:
REM Windows Search service to Manual (elevated)
sc config WSearch start=demand
net stop WSearch
REM back to automatic if you miss instant search:
REM sc config WSearch start=auto && net start WSearch
demo.how_to_run: Run in an elevated Command Prompt

steps: services.msc > Windows Search > set Startup type to Manual (or Disabled) and Stop it
Alternative: Indexing Options > Modify > uncheck the SSD, keep HDDs indexed
Search still works — it just searches live instead of from an index
expected_gain: Less background disk/CPU; fewer SSD writes
risk: Low — file searches become slightly slower but stay functional
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Keep Windows Updated — Strategically
overview: Updates bring security fixes and sometimes performance. The strategy: install them promptly, but pause for a week when a bad patch is in the news, and never interrupt an install.

demo.code:
# Update status from the shell (PowerShell)
# last installed updates:
Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select -First 10 HotFixID, InstalledOn
# pending reboot?
Test-Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WindowsUpdate\Auto Update\RebootRequired"
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell

steps: Settings > Windows Update: install available updates weekly
If a bad patch is widely reported: Pause updates for 1-2 weeks, then resume
Keep drivers OUT of Windows Update if you manage GPU drivers manually (optional advanced)
After major feature updates: check Disk Cleanup > "Previous Windows installations" to reclaim space

commands.check: Settings > Windows Update > Check for updates
commands.cleanup: cleanmgr.exe > Clean up system files > Previous Windows installations

expected_gain: Security + occasional performance fixes; avoids bad-patch downtime
risk: Low
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Clean Install Windows: The Fresh-Start Checklist
title: Clean Install Windows: The Fresh-Start Checklist
overview: When years of cruft resist all tuning, a clean install restores factory-fresh speed. The checklist matters more than the install: backups, drivers, and keys first.

demo.code:
# Pre-wipe backup checklist (PowerShell) — verify BEFORE installing
$docs = "$env:USERPROFILE\Documents"
Write-Output "Documents: $docs ($(Get-ChildItem $docs -Recurse -File -EA SilentlyContinue | Measure-Object).Count files)"
# export installed program list:
Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*" | Where-Object DisplayName | Select DisplayName, DisplayVersion | Export-Csv "$env:USERPROFILE\Desktop\programs-before.csv"
Write-Output "Program list saved to Desktop. Copy it + your files to backup NOW."
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell before wiping — the CSV is your reinstall list

steps: Back up: documents, browser profiles, game saves, license keys, and a driver folder (chipset/GPU/LAN/Wi-Fi)
Create install media: Microsoft Media Creation Tool on an 8 GB+ USB
Boot USB, delete old partitions (or install fresh on a new SSD), install
Install drivers in order: chipset, LAN/Wi-Fi, GPU, audio, rest
Restore files; reinstall apps from Ninite/winget for speed
expected_gain: Often the fastest the PC has ever felt — all cruft gone
risk: High — total data loss if backup is incomplete; verify backups open before wiping
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Dust Cleaning and Thermal Maintenance Schedule
title: Dust Cleaning and Thermal Maintenance Schedule
overview: Dust is a slow performance killer: it insulates heatsinks, chokes fans, and raises temperatures until throttling steals speed. A simple calendar beats every emergency clean.

demo.code:
@echo off
REM Dust-maintenance log (append a line each cleaning)
set LOG=%USERPROFILE%\Desktop\pc-maintenance.log
echo %date% %time% - Dust clean done >> "%LOG%"
echo Logged to pc-maintenance.log. Suggested cadence: quick check every 3 months.
demo.how_to_run: Save as dustlog.bat; run after each cleaning to keep the schedule

steps: Every 3 months: visual check through the case window; quick blow-out of intake filters
Every 6-12 months: full clean — compressed air on heatsinks/fans (hold blades), wipe filters
Every 2-3 years: repaste CPU/GPU if temperatures crept up
Laptops: clean vents; consider a cooling pad if it runs hot on desks

commands.monitor: HWiNFO64 — log temps before/after cleaning to prove the gain
commands.filters: Washable filters: rinse, dry fully, reinstall

expected_gain: 5-15C lower temps; fans quieter; throttling eliminated
risk: Low — unplug first; hold fan blades while blowing
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: BIOS/UEFI Speed Settings: XMP and Fast Boot
title: BIOS/UEFI Speed Settings: XMP and Fast Boot
overview: Two BIOS toggles with real impact: XMP/DOCP runs your RAM at its rated speed (it defaults slower), and Fast Boot skips redundant checks. Both are safe on stable systems.

demo.code:
# Verify RAM is actually running at XMP speed (PowerShell)
Get-CimInstance Win32_PhysicalMemory | Select Speed, ConfiguredClockSpeed
# Compare Speed to the rating on the box. If it shows 2133/2400 on 3200-rated RAM, XMP is off.
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell after enabling XMP

steps: Enter BIOS (Del/F2 at boot)
Enable XMP (Intel) or DOCP/EXPO (AMD) — RAM runs at advertised speed
Enable Fast Boot (skips some POST checks)
Save & Exit; verify in Task Manager > Memory that speed matches the box

commands.enter: Del / F2 / F12 at boot (varies by board)
commands.reset: Clear CMOS if the system becomes unstable

expected_gain: RAM bandwidth up 20-40% vs JEDEC defaults; a few seconds off boot
risk: Medium — unstable XMP causes crashes; disable if problems appear
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Trim Fonts and Language Packs
overview: Hundreds of installed fonts and unused language packs slow font enumeration and waste space. Removing the obvious extras is safe and quick.

demo.code:
# Count installed fonts + languages (PowerShell)
(Get-ChildItem "$env:SystemRoot\Fonts" -File).Count
Get-WinUserLanguageList | Select LanguageTag, Autonym
# remove a language (example):
# $l = Get-WinUserLanguageList; $l.RemoveAll({$_.LanguageTag -eq "fr-FR"}); Set-WinUserLanguageList $l -Force
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell

steps: Settings > Personalization > Fonts: remove fonts you never use (keep system fonts)
Settings > Time & language > Language: remove languages you do not read
Disk Cleanup > Clean up system files: check "Language resource files" if offered
expected_gain: Small but real: faster app font menus, some disk space
risk: Low — keep at least your system language and default fonts
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Cloud Sync Tuning: OneDrive and Dropbox
title: Cloud Sync Tuning: OneDrive and Dropbox
overview: Cloud sync clients can pin disk and CPU re-indexing thousands of files. Files On-Demand plus selective sync keeps the convenience without the constant churn.

demo.code:
# OneDrive sync state + storage use (PowerShell)
Get-Process OneDrive -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select Name, CPU
$od = "$env:USERPROFILE\OneDrive"
if (Test-Path $od) { $gb=[math]::Round((Get-ChildItem $od -Recurse -File -EA SilentlyContinue | Measure-Object Length -Sum).Sum/1GB,2); Write-Output "Local OneDrive cache: $gb GB" }
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell

steps: OneDrive Settings: enable Files On-Demand (files download only when opened)
Choose folders: sync only what you need (Settings > Account > Choose folders)
Pause syncing during gaming/heavy work (taskbar icon > Pause)
Dropbox: same — Smart Sync + selective sync

commands.onedemand: OneDrive Settings > Sync and backup > Advanced > Files On-Demand

expected_gain: Less background disk/CPU; faster boot
risk: Low — files stay in the cloud; know what is local before going offline
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Network Throughput Tuning
overview: Slow downloads are usually ISP or Wi-Fi — but stale DNS, bufferbloat, and auto-tuning glitches are fixable locally. Tune in order: DNS, adapter, then router.

demo.code:
REM Network tune-up (elevated)
netsh int tcp set global autotuninglevel=normal
ipconfig /flushdns
REM show current TCP settings:
netsh int tcp show global
REM quick latency check:
ping -n 10 1.1.1.1
demo.how_to_run: Run in an elevated Command Prompt

steps: Speed test wired vs Wi-Fi to isolate (fast.com / speedtest.net)
Set fast DNS: 1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8 on the adapter
Elevated: netsh int tcp set global autotuninglevel=normal (fixes some slow cases)
Router: enable QoS/SQM if gaming while others stream; update router firmware
Wi-Fi: use 5 GHz near the router; Ethernet for anything stationary

commands.autotune: netsh int tcp set global autotuninglevel=normal

expected_gain: Lower latency; full ISP speed actually reached
risk: Low
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Disable Visual Effects for Speed
overview: Animations and transparency cost GPU cycles on weak integrated graphics. Turning them off makes old PCs feel noticeably snappier.

demo.code:
# Toggle visual effects via registry (current user)
# Best performance preset:
Set-ItemProperty "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\VisualEffects" -Name VisualFXSetting -Value 2 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Set-ItemProperty "HKCU:\Control Panel\Desktop\WindowMetrics" -Name MinAnimate -Value 0
Write-Output "Log off and back on to apply."
demo.how_to_run: Run in PowerShell, then log off/on

Or custom: keep only "Smooth edges of screen fonts" and "Show thumbnails"
Settings > Personalization > Colors: Transparency effects off
expected_gain: Snappier UI on weak GPUs; tiny battery savings
risk: Low — purely cosmetic
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Weekly Maintenance Script
overview: One scheduled script that does the boring upkeep — temp cleanup, update check nudge, health report — beats remembering. Automate the routine.

demo.code:
@echo off
REM Weekly maintenance (run elevated)
set LOG=%TEMP%\maint.log
echo === %date% %time% === >> "%LOG%"
del /Q /F "%TEMP%\*" 2>nul >> "%LOG%"
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup >> "%LOG%" 2>&1
sfc /verifyonly >> "%LOG%" 2>&1
wmic diskdrive get model,status >> "%LOG%" 2>&1

steps: Save the script below as weekly-maint.bat
Test it once manually (elevated)
Task Scheduler: run weekly, "Run with highest privileges"
Review its log monthly

commands.schedule: Task Scheduler > Create Task > Weekly trigger

risk: Low — the script only cleans temps and reports
provenance: Standard PC optimization procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Battery vs Performance Balance on Laptops
title: Battery vs Performance Balance on Laptops
overview: Laptops live on a slider between speed and battery. Set it deliberately per situation instead of leaving it wherever it landed.

Plugged in for work: "Best performance"

title: Malware Scan Routine

Monthly: Windows Security full scan + Malwarebytes Free scan
After any scare: Defender Offline scan (reboots into a clean environment)
Keep real-time protection ON; decline "free trials" that nag

commands.offline: Windows Security > Scan options > Microsoft Defender Offline scan
